Subject: Re: Discovery call recap (initial-emit targets)

Thanks for the call today — good alignment overall. To recap from our side:
- Goal: integrate Redwood for product description generation in checkout flows. Critical metric is perceived latency at checkout (we want no visible stalls).
- Targets (what we'd like to validate in the engineering trial): 95th percentile time-to-first-token (TTFT) <= 120ms for common prompt shapes; typical prompt payloads ~1–2k tokens.
- Throughput: steady-state ~150 QPS across peak regions (NA), with capacity to burst to ~700 QPS for flash sales.
- Streaming preference: SSE preferred (browser clients, simpler reconnection) but we have a small WebSocket desktop client for internal tooling. Chunk cadence: aim for first emit quickly (single-token priming acceptable) then 2–4 chunks delivered within 200–400ms windows.

Open questions we promised to answer:
1) What pilot measurement windows and telemetry will Redwood provide?
2) Warm-start / cache priming options to hit TTFT consistently.
3) Any recommended client-side fallbacks (heartbeat, small initial placeholder) if TTFT spikes.

Next step from our side: schedule the 2-week engineering trial starting as early as July 6. We'll provide an access test account and sample prompts.

—Chris
FastRetail — Sr. Product Manager

Hi Chris / Sara — thanks for the clear targets and for proposing dates. Short recap and what we'll run in the 2-week trial:

Summary of what Redwood will validate during trial:
- TTFT objective: measure and aim for 95th <= 120ms for the provided representative prompts; we'll surface p50/p95/p99 and per-region breakdown.
- Throughput/concurrency: we will run synthetic and replay-driven traffic to validate 150 QPS steady-state and bursts up to 700 QPS.
- Streaming transport: we'll run parallel SSE and WebSocket experiments. Expect SSE to have slightly lower client switching overhead; WS may show lower per-connection handshake cost under certain browser conditions.
- Chunk cadence experiments: start with aggressive first-emit (seed token) then 200–350 token chunk targets; we'll also test smaller 80–150 token cadence to compare perceived latency vs payload frequency.

What we need from FastRetail before trial start (ideally by June 28):
1) Sample prompt set (100 representative requests) and distribution of payload sizes.
2) Target client platforms / browsers (Chrome mobile, iOS Safari, internal desktop) so we can instrument proper handshake/latency probes.
3) Any network egress restrictions or IP allowlist needs.

Deliverables Redwood will provide:
- A pilot plan (attached: redwood-ttft-guardrails-v1.pdf) with exact probe shapes and measurement script.
- Pre-configured telemetry dashboard (OpenTelemetry hooks + token-level cost breakdown).
- A small probe script (pilot-probe-script.sh) to run from your staging cluster to replay traffic.

Engineer's note: Neha will lead the trial instrumentation and will propose a two-day warmup window that focuses on model warm-start and KV priming. We expect the warm-start to materially improve p95 TTFT for repeated prompt patterns.

- Jun 28: FastRetail drops prompt set + allowlist info

Subject: Re: Post-call: engineering trial for initial-emit SLAs and chunk cadence

Hi Chris — quick technical follow-up with clarifying requests and a proposed measurement plan.

Key clarifications we need to run reproducible probes:
- Prompt shapes: are prompts mostly short templates (50–150 tokens) with context embedding, or long user-provided text (~1–2k tokens)? Please tag the 100-sample set with "short" vs "long".
- Concurrency pattern: is the 150 QPS steady-state coming from many concurrent users (~1k users at low QPS), or fewer long-lived connections (200 active WebSocket clients)? This changes whether we bias toward connection warm-start or per-request cold path.
- Allowed response size: typical generation length per request (avg/95th) — helps size chunk cadence.

Proposed pilot measurement plan (week-by-week):
Week 0 (pre-trial): set up allowlist, telemetry endpoints, and run small smoke tests (single-digit QPS)
Week 1 (warm-up, 3 days + 4 days of measured baseline):
  - Day 1–2: Warm-start runs to exercise model cache (KV priming) and measure improvement curve.
  - Day 3–7: Baseline measured at 150 QPS replayed from your staging traffic. Capture p50/p95/p99 TTFT and first-chunk size timing.
Week 2 (stress & transport experiments):
  - Transport A: SSE-focused run at target QPS with chunk cadence A (first emit + 300-token chunks).
  - Transport B: WebSocket-focused run, smaller 120-token chunks, more frequent heartbeats.
  - Stress run: 700 QPS burst for 10 minutes to confirm graceful degradation and fallback behavior.

Engineering knobs we'll exercise:
- Warm-start persistence window (30s, 2min, 10min) to show TTFT delta.
- Batch sizing & micro-batching thresholds to hit latency vs throughput tradeoffs.
- KV cache priming (seed examples on session start) to lower first-token cost for templated prompts.

Client fallbacks we recommend during trial:
- If first emit > 250ms, show a lightweight spinner + render partial placeholder and use subsequent chunk merges.
- Exponential reconnect backoff for SSE with jitter; identical fallback to WebSocket with immediate small-chunk probe once ws reconnect completes.

Telemetry we will surface (examples):
- Per-request TTFT histogram (p50/p95/p99), first-chunk latency, per-chunk timing, token throughput, and connection handshakes.
- Alert rule: sustained p95 TTFT > 220ms for 5m triggers engineer paging.

Questions for you to confirm:
1) Are you comfortable with Redwood running a stress burst to 700 QPS during Week 2 (we'll coordinate precise timing)?
2) Will you provide access to a staging client (or synthetic runner) that mimics your browser mix?

If those are ok I'll schedule the warm-up and upload the telemetry dashboard.

Best — Neha
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
